contributes.instructions: The css-author plugin contributes two gates, which `lint` runs over the project's pages and `draft_finalize` over the page it is about to write, their findings blocking (a finalize refused, nothing written) save the few they mark advisory: the static lint (facts from a page's markup and stylesheets — a length with no unit, a restated initial value, a font face nothing names, a class no rule names, a stray `;` that makes the browser drop the rule after it — and what matching the page decides: a rule that matches nothing, a declaration another already makes, a container query no ancestor can answer) and the necessity lint (each declaration removed in the rendered page and restored; one that changes no element's geometry or computed style at the viewport's width nor at a sweep of other widths is dead). Their findings name an element by its unique selector, and a rule by its selector as written and the stylesheet it is written in — the project file, or the page's `<style>` block — which is the one to edit; a read-only stylesheet's rules (a remote one, or a file Daydream cannot write) are never a finding's subject. A stylesheet other pages link too is judged only on the pages the gates render (at a finalize, the draft's page alone; under `lint {viewportIds}`, those viewports'), so what they find of its rules — a rule that matches nothing, a declaration that changes nothing or restates another — is advisory there, naming the pages not judged: never delete such a rule for it without checking those pages. Treat their findings as the Core tools section says. A viewport is authored as a draft the user watches take shape: draft_open is the FIRST call of the task — the frame, the title and the html › body skeleton with its page background (never a page without one), sent before knowledge_bundle, before any reading, before planning — then knowledge_bundle {query: <the task in a few words>} ONCE (it returns the format rules with the example nearest the task), then one visual group per draft_append as each is written — its markup and the css it needs, a rule the group shares sent with it — then draft_finalize, which writes it into the project's files once the gates pass. A refusal's findings name what to fix and where: what the draft wrote is fixed in the draft, and a finding in a stylesheet file that was there before the draft is fixed in that file, never during a variant round; then finalize again. At a variant's finalize the gates refuse only what the variant causes — its own css and the rules it writes or changes in the `<style>` blocks (re-indenting or splitting a block changes none), judged as its page will read them once accepted, and the classes and inline declarations it adds; what they find in the page's own stylesheets, in the rules of its `<style>` blocks the variant keeps, or in markup the page already has (wherever the variant moves or wraps it), is advisory there, and stays as it is. A line of the page's that the variant leaves dead once accepted is said too — one its css overrides at some width, or whose element it removes: the next in-place rework of the page refuses it until it is removed from its file, and so does `lint` when the accept appends the css to a stylesheet other pages link. The layout procedures (which formatting context, whether a declaration is needed at all, where in the cascade it goes) are this plugin's: read them once per task with knowledge_read {path: "mrbavio.css-author/procedures.md"} (or the `procedures` resource) and judge every declaration by them. The author → finalize → fix workflow is Daydream's own dream-author prompt: start every document task from it.
